HIV‐1 infection induces a state of immune dysfunction that is characterized by a progressive loss of CD4 T cells and an increased rate of apoptosis of CD4 T lymphocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms that regulate T‐cell homeostasis in HIV‐1‐infected individuals, and how these mechanisms are altered by highly active antiretorviral therapy.
the mechanisms of HIV‐induced immune suppression.
the molecular mechanisms of the pathophysiology of AIDS, and with the development of novel strategies to prevent and treat HIV‐1 infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HIV‐1‐specific CD8+ T cell response is not impaired during ART.
the HIV‐1 infection is not a direct cause for the T‐lymphocyte depletion, but rather a consequence of the immune response.
the effect of HIV on the immune system is complex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated the importance of the balance between pro‐ and anti‐apoptotic cytokines in the maintenance of peripheral T‐cell homeostasis during HIV‐1 infection and that this balance is perturbed by antiretrovirus therapy.
the immune system is capable of responding to HIV‐1 infection and can be stimulated by therapeutic agents to produce an effective immune response.
the T‐cell response is more complex than we had thought and the mechanisms of HIV‐1‐specific CD8 T‐cell responses are more diverse and dynamic than previously appreciated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
T cells from HIV‐1‐infected patients are protected against spontaneous apoptosis by the production of endogenous cytokines.
the HIV‐induced depletion of T cells is not a passive event, but rather an active process that is regulated by the immune system itself.

, in the setting of HIV‐1 infection, the balance between pro‐ and anti‐apoptotic factors determines the extent of T‐cell apoptosis, and that this balance is modulated in the context of antiviral therapy.
